q: Movie studios use powerful computers to create special effects and animations. This is an application of computers in:
exp:
Special effects and animation in movies is an entertainment application of computers.
★ Exam Points:
• CGI (Computer Generated Imagery) is used in movies.
• Animation software: Maya, Blender.
• Gaming and streaming are also entertainment uses.

q: Which of the following characteristics represents the ability of a computer to work continuously without fatigue?
exp:
Diligence is the ability to work continuously without fatigue or loss of concentration.
★ Exam Points:
• Diligence = no tiredness or boredom.
• Humans lose concentration; computers do not.
• Related: consistency in repeated tasks.

q: Which characteristic of computers enables them to perform various tasks such as calculations, graphics, and communication?
exp:
Versatility is the ability to perform many different kinds of tasks (calculation, graphics, communication).
★ Exam Points:
• Versatility – a single computer can do word processing, gaming, design, communication.
• Computers are general-purpose machines.
• Special-purpose computers do one task only.

q: What do you mean by .wma file on the computer?
exp:
The .wma extension means Windows Media Audio format.
★ Exam Points:
• .wma – Windows Media Audio (Microsoft).
• .mp3 – MPEG-1 Audio Layer 3.
• .wav – uncompressed audio.

q: A computer performs millions of calculations in a fraction of a second. Which characteristic is primarily demonstrated here?
exp:
Doing millions of calculations in a fraction of a second shows speed.
★ Exam Points:
• Speed is the most prominent characteristic of a computer.
• Speed measured in MHz/GHz for processors.
• FLOPS measure floating-point speed.

q: The term GIGO (Garbage In Garbage Out) is most closely related to which computer characteristic?
exp:
GIGO means the quality of output depends on the input; it relates to accuracy, since correct results need correct input.
★ Exam Points:
• GIGO – Garbage In Garbage Out.
• Computers are accurate if input and program are correct.
• Most errors are human errors.

q: Which characteristic of a computer ensures that identical input and instructions always produce the same output?
exp:
Consistency means identical input and instructions always yield the same output.
★ Exam Points:
• Consistency/reliability – same input → same output.
• Computers have no emotions or fatigue.
• Deterministic behaviour helps testing.

q: In the field of e-commerce and financial trading, which application of computers is essential for analyzing massive volumes of rapidly changing market data and detecting complex patterns to inform investment decisions?
exp:
Real-time predictive analytics analyses fast-changing market data to detect patterns in e-commerce and trading.
★ Exam Points:
• Predictive analytics uses data mining and machine learning.
• Real-time analytics processes streaming data.
• Used in stock trading and fraud detection.

q: Who is widely regarded as the ‘Father of Computers’ for designing the first mechanical computing device?
exp:
Charles Babbage is called the Father of Computers for his Difference Engine and Analytical Engine.
★ Exam Points:
• Babbage designed the Difference Engine (1822) and Analytical Engine (1837).
• Ada Lovelace is the first computer programmer.
• Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline adding machine (1642).

q: The fourth generation of computers marked the use of integrated circuits and compact computing. This generation began with the invention of which key component?
exp:
The fourth generation (1971 onwards) began with the invention of the microprocessor, which placed the whole CPU on a single VLSI chip.
★ Exam Points:
• First microprocessor: Intel 4004 (1971).
• Transistors were used in the 2nd generation.
• ENIAC was a 1st-generation computer.

q: Unlike humans, a computer does not feel tired or bored while repeating the same task all day. This shows which characteristic?
exp:
Diligence: a computer does not feel tired, bored or lose concentration when repeating a task.
★ Exam Points:
• Diligence – works for hours without tiredness.
• Versatility – performs many types of tasks.
• Accuracy – gives error-free results with correct input.

q: In which year was the world’s first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, launched?
exp:
Intel launched the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, in 1971.
★ Exam Points:
• Intel 4004 was a 4-bit processor designed by Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin and Stanley Mazor.
• It had about 2,300 transistors.
• Intel 8080 (1974) and 8086 (1978) came later.

q: Which indigenous microprocessor, launched in 2025, marked a milestone in India’s technological self- reliance as the country’s first 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core processor?
exp:
DHRUV64 is India's first indigenous 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core microprocessor, from C-DAC under the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) programme, 2025.
★ Exam Points:
• DHRUV64 was developed by C-DAC under the Microprocessor Development Programme (Digital India RISC-V).
• Other Indian processors: SHAKTI (IIT Madras), VEGA (C-DAC), AJIT (IIT Bombay).
• VIKRAM 3201 is ISRO-SCL's 32-bit space-grade processor.

q: Which of the following demonstrates the use of computers in scientific research?
exp:
Simulation of experiments is a scientific research use of computers.
★ Exam Points:
• Simulation models weather, nuclear reactions and drug interactions.
• Supercomputers like PARAM are used in research.
• CAD/CAM is used in engineering design.

q: Which sector uses computers for online transactions, payroll processing, inventory control, and data analysis?
exp:
Business and commerce use computers for online transactions, payroll, inventory control and data analysis.
★ Exam Points:
• Banks use computers for core banking, ATMs and online transactions.
• Payroll and inventory are classic business data-processing tasks.
• E-commerce = buying and selling online.

q: Which major technological advancement characterizes the fourth generation of computers?
exp:
The fourth generation of computers (1971 onwards) used microprocessors (VLSI chips).
★ Exam Points:
• 4th generation began 1971 with Intel 4004 (VLSI).
• 3rd generation used Integrated Circuits (ICs).
• 5th generation is based on Artificial Intelligence and ULSI.

q: A major characteristic of computer systems is Diligence. Which of the following scenarios primarily highlights a limitation of the computer system that is not overcome by its diligence?
o: A computer is used to book flights in the morning and write code in the afternoon.
A computer performs trillions of calculations a second, much faster than any human.
A computer continues processing data for 72 hours straight without any loss of attention.
A computer generates incorrect output because the initial data entered was flawed.
exp:
Diligence means a computer does not tire. A limitation such as having no intelligence of its own (it only follows instructions) is not removed by diligence.
★ Exam Points:
• GIGO – Garbage In, Garbage Out: wrong input gives wrong output.
• Computers have no IQ (no intelligence of their own).
• Diligence = no fatigue or loss of concentration.

q: Which characteristic of a computer system enables it to perform extremely complex calculations within seconds?
exp:
Speed lets a computer perform complex calculations in seconds, in nano- or microseconds per operation.
★ Exam Points:
• Computer speed is measured in micro/nano/pico seconds, MIPS or FLOPS.
• Supercomputer speed is measured in FLOPS.
• 1 nanosecond = 10⁻⁹ second.

q: Preparation of report cards, maintaining student records, and creating question papers are actions that are mainly related to which area of computer application?
exp:
Report cards, student records and question papers are administrative tasks in education.
★ Exam Points:
• e-Governance in education: DigiLocker stores mark sheets.
• School MIS software maintains student records.
• Computer-Based Tests (CBT) are used by SSC and RRB.

q: Which computer application is mainly used for booking railway tickets and flight reservations?
exp:
Railway and flight booking use reservation systems.
★ Exam Points:
• Railway reservation: PRS / IRCTC.
• Airline reservation systems: GDS (Amadeus, Sabre).
• Reservation systems run on online databases.

q: Which of the following numbers is used to represent the ASCII value of the uppercase letter 'B'?
exp:
ASCII codes: 'A' = 65, so uppercase 'B' = 66. Lowercase 'a' = 97.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII 'A' = 65, 'Z' = 90, 'a' = 97, 'z' = 122, '0' = 48.
• Standard ASCII is 7-bit (128 characters).
• Space character = 32.

q: Which of the following statements is true regarding ASCII, LAN, and CD in computer terminology?
o: LAN refers to a wide geographical network like the internet.
CD is a rewritable magnetic storage medium.
ASCII is used for formatting disks in a LAN network.
ASCII represents characters using numeric codes in binary.
exp:
ASCII is a character encoding standard; LAN is a local network and a CD is an optical (not rewritable magnetic) medium.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII encodes characters as numbers.
• LAN is a local network.
• CD is optical storage.

q: With reference to computing, what does ASCII stand for?
o: American Standard Code for Information Integrity
American Systematic Code for International Interoperability
Algorithmic Standard Code for International Information
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
exp:
ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII developed in 1963 by ANSI.
• 7-bit code with 128 characters.
• Unicode supports all world scripts.

q: A computer's characteristic of Accuracy means it can produce precise and correct results as long as the _________________ is/are correct.
exp:
Accuracy means results are correct as long as the input data and instructions are correct (GIGO).
★ Exam Points:
• Accuracy depends on correct data and programs.
• GIGO principle.
• Hardware rarely makes calculation errors.

q: Which of the following applications are supercomputers primarily used for?
exp:
Supercomputers are used mainly for complex mathematical calculations such as weather modelling and nuclear simulation.
★ Exam Points:
• Supercomputers: weather forecasting, nuclear simulation, climate research.
• India's PARAM series by C-DAC (PARAM 8000 in 1991).
• Speed measured in FLOPS (petaflops/exaflops).

q: Which of the following is an example of computers in the service industry?
exp:
Automated ticket booking is a service-industry application of computers.
★ Exam Points:
• Service industry: banking, railways, airlines, hotels, telecom.
• IRCTC is India's railway ticket booking system.
• Manufacturing uses CAM and robots.

q: The statement "A computer can work tirelessly and consistently for long periods without losing concentration" represents which characteristics of the computer?
exp:
Working tirelessly and consistently for long periods is diligence.
★ Exam Points:
• Diligence = consistency without fatigue.
• Accuracy = correctness.
• Speed = time taken.

q: Which characteristic enables a computer to start and complete tasks automatically without human intervention once programmed?
exp:
Automation means that once a program is given, the computer carries out the whole task automatically without further human intervention.
★ Exam Points:
• Automation is possible because of the stored-program concept.
• Diligence = no fatigue.
• Robots and industrial controls use automation.

q: As computer generations progressed, which of the following has been a trend that is generally true?
exp:
Over the generations, computers became smaller, faster, cheaper and more powerful.
★ Exam Points:
• Each generation became smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable.
• Power consumption and heat decreased.
• Vacuum tube → Transistor → IC → Microprocessor → AI.

q: Which computing pioneer is credited with the concept of the "stored program architecture" (where both program instructions and data are held in the same memory), a design that forms the basis of nearly all modern computers?
exp:
John von Neumann proposed the stored-program architecture, where instructions and data share the same memory.
★ Exam Points:
• Von Neumann described the stored-program concept in the EDVAC report (1945).
• Most modern computers follow von Neumann architecture.
• Harvard architecture uses separate memories for data and instructions.

q: Which of the following machines was designed by Charles Babbage?
exp:
Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine (and earlier the Difference Engine).
★ Exam Points:
• Analytical Engine had a "mill" (CPU) and "store" (memory).
• It used punched cards for input.
• Never fully built in Babbage's lifetime.

q: Which computer application enables real-time inventory tracking using automated identification?
exp:
RFID-driven supply chain systems provide real-time inventory tracking through automated identification.
★ Exam Points:
• RFID = Radio Frequency Identification.
• Used in FASTag tolls and supply chains.
• Tags can be passive or active.

q: In which field are computers used for tasks like weather forecasting, simulation, and research?
exp:
Weather forecasting, simulation and research are done with computers in space and meteorology.
★ Exam Points:
• IMD uses supercomputers (Pratyush, Mihir, Arka, Arunika) for forecasting.
• ISRO uses computers for satellite tracking.
• Simulations reduce real-world testing cost.

q: Which computer application category is most crucial for designing complex physical objects like cars, buildings, and machinery before they are built?
exp:
Computer-Aided Design (CAD) is used to design cars, buildings and machinery before they are built.
★ Exam Points:
• CAD software: AutoCAD, SolidWorks, CATIA.
• CAM – Computer-Aided Manufacturing.
• CAD replaces manual drafting.

q: Which of the following was the first electromechanical computer?
exp:
The Harvard Mark I (1944, Howard Aiken, built with IBM) was the first electromechanical computer; ENIAC was the first general-purpose electronic computer.
★ Exam Points:
• Harvard Mark I (ASCC) was built by Howard Aiken with IBM in 1944.
• ENIAC (1946) was the first electronic general-purpose computer.
• UNIVAC I (1951) was the first commercial computer.

q: Information Interchange Extended ASCII, an 8-bit evolution of the original 7-bit ASCII standard, supports international text by expanding the character set. How many total codes does it provide?
exp:
Extended ASCII uses 8 bits and so has 256 codes, including accented characters.
★ Exam Points:
• 7-bit ASCII = 2⁷ = 128 codes.
• 8-bit extended ASCII = 2⁸ = 256 codes.
• Unicode UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes.

q: Which digital file format is widely used to save three-dimensional models for 3D printing? It is the standard format supported by most 3D printers.
exp:
STL (stereolithography) is the standard file format for 3D printing.
★ Exam Points:
• STL = stereolithography / Standard Tessellation Language.
• 3D printing is additive manufacturing.
• Other 3D formats: OBJ, 3MF.

q: What does the abbreviation EBCDIC stand for?
o: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
Encoded Binary Character Data Interchange Code
Electronic Binary Code for Data Interchange Communication
Extended Binary Code for Digital Information Communication
exp:
EBCDIC stands for Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code, an 8-bit IBM code.
★ Exam Points:
• EBCDIC was developed by IBM for mainframes.
• EBCDIC is an 8-bit code (256 characters).
• BCD = Binary Coded Decimal.

q: What does ASCII stand for?
o: Automated System for Computer Information Interchange
Advanced Standard Coding in Information Industry
Auxiliary System for Communication and Interchange
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
exp:
ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII is a character-encoding standard.
• Used in computers and communication.
• Unicode's first 128 codes match ASCII.

q: What does the abbreviation ASCII stand for?
o: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Automated System for Computer Integrated Information
exp:
ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
• 'A' = 65.
• Extended ASCII = 256 characters.

q: Identify the correct combination of the abbreviation, its full form and its application.
o: ASCII – American Standard Code for Information Interchange – Encodes text in computers
LAN – Large Area Network – Used for connecting computers across continents
ASCII – Automated Symbolic Code for Integrated Input – Converts images to code
CD – Compact Disk – Used for high-speed internet access
exp:
ASCII – American Standard Code for Information Interchange – is used to represent text characters as numeric codes in computers.
★ Exam Points:
• LAN = Local Area Network (not Large).
• CD = Compact Disc (optical storage, not Internet).
• ASCII 'A' = 65.

q: Which of the following abbreviations is correctly matched with its meaning?
o: ASCII – Automated System for Computer Input
exp:
CD stands for Compact Disc; the other options give wrong expansions for ASCII and LAN.
★ Exam Points:
• CD – Compact Disc; LAN – Local Area Network.
• ASCII – American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
• Always verify full forms carefully.

q: Which of the following correctly pairs the abbreviation with its full form and primary function?
o: CD – Central Disc – Stores operating system permanently
LAN – Local Area Network – Connects computers within a limited area
ASCII – American Standard Communication for Input and Interface – Used for graphic design
ASCII – Advanced System for Communication Interface – Used in LAN setup
exp:
LAN stands for Local Area Network, which connects computers within a limited area such as an office or building. The other options give wrong full forms or functions.
★ Exam Points:
• CD = Compact Disc; ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
• LAN connects computers in a limited area.
• Always check both full form and function in pair questions.

q: A computer system mainly includes which three components?
exp:
A computer system works on the cycle Input, Processing, Output (with storage as an added stage).
★ Exam Points:
• IPO cycle: Input → Process → Output (+ Storage).
• Input devices: keyboard, mouse; output: monitor, printer.
• Processing is done by the CPU.

q: What is the storage size of each ASCII character in bits?
exp:
Standard ASCII is a 7-bit code, but each character is stored in one byte (8 bits); extended ASCII uses all 8 bits.
★ Exam Points:
• 7-bit ASCII = 128 characters.
• Extended ASCII = 256 characters.
• Unicode UTF-16 uses 16 bits.

q: Which type of computer is also known as a notebook?
exp:
A laptop is a portable personal computer, also called a notebook computer.
★ Exam Points:
• Laptops run on rechargeable batteries.
• Smaller forms: netbook, ultrabook, tablet.
• Laptops are a type of microcomputer.

q: Which generation of computers used transistors for the first time?
exp:
Second-generation computers (about 1956–1963) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making them smaller, faster and more reliable.
★ Exam Points:
• Transistor invented at Bell Labs (1947) by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley.
• 1st gen: vacuum tubes; 3rd: ICs; 4th: microprocessors (VLSI).
• High-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL came in the 2nd generation.

q:
Identify whether the following statements are true or false.
(i) ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
(ii) PAN stands for Private Area Network.
(iii) LED stands for Light Emitting Display.
exp:
Only (i) is correct; PAN is Personal Area Network and LED is Light Emitting Diode.
★ Exam Points:
• ASCII is a 7-bit code (128 characters).
• PAN range is about 10 metres (Bluetooth).
• OLED – Organic Light Emitting Diode.

q:
Match List-I (abbreviations) with List-II (full forms).
(a) CD-ROM (b) EEPROM (c) USB (d) PCB
(i) Printed Circuit Board (ii) Compact Disc Read Only Memory (iii) Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory (iv) Universal Serial Bus
exp:
CD-ROM = Compact Disc Read Only Memory, EEPROM = Electrically Erasable PROM, USB = Universal Serial Bus, PCB = Printed Circuit Board.
★ Exam Points:
• EEPROM is erased electrically; EPROM by UV light.
• Motherboard is a large PCB.
• USB introduced in 1996.

q: What is the full form of EDVAC?
exp:
EDVAC – Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer – was one of the first stored-program computers, described by John von Neumann (1945).
★ Exam Points:
• EDVAC used binary instead of decimal (ENIAC used decimal).
• EDSAC (1949, Cambridge) was the first practical stored-program computer.
• Von Neumann architecture stores data and program in the same memory.

q:
Match the abbreviations with their full forms.
(a) LCD (b) ISP (c) SRAM (d) PCB
(i) Printed Circuit Board (ii) Liquid Crystal Display (iii) Internet Service Provider (iv) Static Random Access Memory
exp:
LCD = Liquid Crystal Display, ISP = Internet Service Provider, SRAM = Static RAM, PCB = Printed Circuit Board.
★ Exam Points:
• SRAM is used for cache; DRAM for main memory.
• Indian ISPs: BSNL, Jio, Airtel.
• LCDs need a backlight; OLED does not.

q: Which generation of computers is characterised by vacuum tubes?
exp:
First-generation computers (1940–1956) used vacuum tubes for circuitry and magnetic drums for memory.
★ Exam Points:
• Examples: ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC I.
• They were huge, consumed much power and produced heat.
• Programmed in machine language.

q: The programming languages C++, COBOL and Java were used in which generation of computers?
exp:
Fourth-generation (microprocessor-based) computers used high-level languages such as C, C++, Java and also COBOL/FORTRAN.
★ Exam Points:
• 1st generation used machine language; 2nd used assembly and early HLLs.
• Java was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (1995).
• C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup (1983).

q: Which was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer designed in the United States for corporate (business) applications?
exp:
UNIVAC I (1951) by Eckert and Mauchly was the first commercial computer, delivered to the US Census Bureau.
★ Exam Points:
• ENIAC (1946) was the first general-purpose electronic computer, built for the US Army.
• Z3 (1941) by Konrad Zuse was an electromechanical computer.
• UNIVAC predicted the 1952 US election result.

q:
Identify whether the given statements related to characteristics of a computer are true or false.
(a) Power of remembrance: a computer can remember data for us.
(b) No IQ: a computer does not work without instructions.
exp:
Both are standard characteristics: computers store and recall data (power of remembrance) and have no intelligence of their own, needing instructions.
★ Exam Points:
• Other characteristics: speed, accuracy, diligence, versatility, storage.
• Diligence = no tiredness or loss of concentration.
• GIGO – Garbage In, Garbage Out.

q: Who is responsible for loading the operating system into memory during the booting process?
exp:
The BIOS (stored in ROM) runs the bootstrap routine that loads the operating system into memory at start-up.
★ Exam Points:
• Booting: POST → bootstrap loader → OS loaded into RAM.
• BIOS firmware is stored in ROM/flash.
• UEFI is the modern replacement for BIOS.

q: Which metric indicates the average number of instructions a CPU executes per clock cycle?
exp:
IPC (Instructions Per Cycle) is the average number of instructions a CPU executes per clock cycle.
★ Exam Points:
• Performance ≈ IPC × clock speed.
• Higher IPC means more work per cycle.
• Clock speed measured in GHz.

q: Physically, a CPU is placed on one or more microchips known as:
exp:
Physically, a CPU is built on one or more microchips called microprocessors.
★ Exam Points:
• Microprocessor = CPU on a single chip.
• First microprocessor: Intel 4004 (1971).
• Modern CPUs contain billions of transistors.

q: What is the primary role of the Control Unit (CU) within the Central Processing Unit (CPU)?
o: It manages and coordinates the flow of instructions and data throughout the computer system.
It performs all the arithmetic and logical calculations on data.
It provides the systems primary volatile storage for active programs.
It permanently stores the operating system and basic boot instructions.
exp:
The Control Unit manages and coordinates the flow of instructions and data in the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• CU coordinates all units of the computer.
• ALU does calculations.
• RAM is primary volatile storage.

q: Which of the following devices functions as both an input and an output device?
exp:
A touchscreen both takes input and shows output.
★ Exam Points:
• Touchscreen is an I/O device.
• Printer and speaker are output; keyboard is input.
• Modem and NIC are also I/O devices.

q: The abbreviation BIOS stands for:
exp:
BIOS stands for Basic Input/Output System.
★ Exam Points:
• BIOS = Basic Input/Output System.
• Performs POST at start-up.
• Enter BIOS setup with F2/Del key.

q: Which type of touchscreen functions by pressing two flexible layers together, allowing it to detect input from a non-conductive object like a fingernail or plastic stylus?
exp:
A resistive touchscreen has two flexible layers pressed together, so it works with a fingernail or plastic stylus; capacitive screens need conductive touch.
★ Exam Points:
• Resistive touch works with any object (pressure-based).
• Capacitive needs a conductive object (finger).
• SAW uses ultrasonic waves.

q: Which of the following devices processes data in the computer system?
exp:
The CPU processes data. FDD and HDD are storage devices and RAM is main memory.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = brain of the computer.
• FDD = Floppy Disk Drive; HDD = Hard Disk Drive.
• RAM holds data temporarily for the CPU.

q: Consider a scenario where a user is interacting with a virtual reality (VR) environment. Which of the following input devices is least likely to be the primary means of navigation and interaction within this immersive environment?
o: Head-mounted display with integrated motion tracking
Optical mouse connected to the computer
exp:
An optical mouse on a desk is least suited to VR navigation, which relies on controllers, head tracking and haptic gloves.
★ Exam Points:
• VR uses head-mounted displays (HMD) with motion tracking.
• Haptic gloves give touch feedback.
• Examples: Meta Quest, Apple Vision Pro.

q: Which of the following accurately explains why a touchscreen can be considered both an input and an output device?
o: It processes user data internally and sends it to memory.
It allows users to interact with visual data and sends touch signals to the computer.
It only displays images but responds to voice commands.
It stores programs and lets users write directly to memory.
exp:
A touchscreen displays visuals (output) and registers the user's touches (input).
★ Exam Points:
• Touchscreen: display (output) + touch sensor (input).
• Capacitive screens sense finger charge.
• Smartphones use capacitive multi-touch.

q: Which of the following best encapsulates the concept of a 'stored-program computer' as introduced by the Von Neumann architecture?
o: A computer that utilises separate memory units for data and instructions to optimise processing speed
A computer that relies primarily on external storage devices for program execution
A computer that can only execute a fixed set of instructions hardwired into its circuitry
A computer where both data and instructions are stored in the same primary memory for sequential execution
exp:
A stored-program computer keeps both instructions and data in the same memory, so the program can be changed without rewiring.
★ Exam Points:
• Stored-program: program can be changed by loading new instructions.
• First stored-program computers: Manchester Baby (1948), EDSAC (1949).
• ENIAC was rewired for new programs (not stored-program initially).

q: What is the main purpose of the Tab key on a standard keyboard?
o: To shift the cursor to the next field or tab position
exp:
The Tab key moves the cursor to the next field or tab stop.
★ Exam Points:
• Tab inserts indentation in text editors.
• In forms, Tab moves to the next field.
• Shift + Tab moves to the previous field.

q: With reference to computer systems, what does CPU stand for?
exp:
CPU stands for Central Processing Unit.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = Central Processing Unit.
• Also called processor or microprocessor.
• Major makers: Intel, AMD, Apple (M-series), Qualcomm.

q: Consider a scenario where a user interacts with a touch-sensitive display. Which of the following best describes the functional duality of this component within a computer system?
o: It acts solely as an output device, displaying visual feedback to the user's actions.
It functions exclusively as an input device, capturing the user's touch gestures and commands.
It serves as both an input device, detecting touch input, and an output device, displaying information and visual responses.
Its primary role is data storage, retaining user interactions for later processing.
exp:
A touch-sensitive display shows visuals (output) and detects touch (input), serving as both.
★ Exam Points:
• Touchscreens combine a display with a touch sensor.
• Types: resistive, capacitive, SAW, infrared.
• Used in ATMs, kiosks and smartphones.

q: Which of the following input devices primarily translates physical, real-world movements into digital signals that can be interpreted by a computer system for tasks such as navigation and object manipulation in a graphical environment?
exp:
The mouse translates physical hand movement into digital signals for pointer control.
★ Exam Points:
• Mouse invented by Douglas Engelbart (1964).
• Optical mice use LED/laser sensors.
• Mouse is a pointing input device.

q: Which of the following statements about Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) is INCORRECT?
o: PCBs serve only desktop computers and not portable devices.
PCBs hold and connect electronic components using conductive tracks.
PCBs provide a base to support and organize hardware parts.
Complex devices may use multilayer PCBs to fit more circuitry.
exp:
PCBs are used in almost all electronic devices – desktops, laptops, mobiles – so saying they serve only desktop computers is incorrect.
★ Exam Points:
• PCB = Printed Circuit Board.
• Copper tracks connect components.
• Multilayer PCBs save space.

q: What does PCB stand for in electronics?
exp:
PCB stands for Printed Circuit Board – a board that mechanically supports and electrically connects electronic components.
★ Exam Points:
• Motherboard is a PCB.
• PCBs are made of fibreglass with copper layers.
• SMT components are soldered on PCBs.

q: What does PCB stand for in electric circuits?
exp:
PCB stands for Printed Circuit Board.
★ Exam Points:
• PCB connects components using copper tracks.
• Motherboard is the main PCB of a computer.
• Multi-layer PCBs are used in complex devices.

q: What is the significance of pipelining in CPU architecture?
o: Increases clock speed using multiple cores
Executes multiple instructions simultaneously by overlapping stages
exp:
Pipelining executes multiple instructions simultaneously by overlapping their fetch, decode and execute stages, increasing instruction throughput.
★ Exam Points:
• Pipelining does not raise clock speed.
• Hazards (data, control) can stall a pipeline.
• Works like an assembly line.

q: In the architecture of a Central Processing Unit (CPU), which statement accurately distinguishes the function of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) from that of the Control Unit (CU)?
o: ALU decodes instructions, while CU handles data storage tasks.
CU executes arithmetic operations, and ALU controls program instructions.
ALU handles calculations and logic functions; CU manages instruction flow and coordination.
CU interacts directly with peripheral devices, and ALU stores temporary data.
exp:
The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations, while the Control Unit manages and coordinates instruction execution and data flow in the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• CU fetches and decodes instructions.
• ALU results are stored in registers/accumulator.
• CU is called the nerve centre of the computer.

q: CMOS, often associated with storing system configuration, stands for:
exp:
CMOS stands for Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor; it stores BIOS settings and is battery-backed.
★ Exam Points:
• CMOS chip is powered by a coin cell battery (CR2032).
• Stores date, time and BIOS settings.
• Removing the battery resets BIOS settings.

q: Consider a scenario where a user is interacting with a graphical application. Which component of the computer system is primarily responsible for rendering the visual elements displayed on the monitor?
exp:
The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) renders visuals on the screen.
★ Exam Points:
• GPU = Graphics Processing Unit (Nvidia, AMD).
• GPUs are also used for AI training.
• VRAM is the GPU's memory.

q: In modern motherboards, which component is directly connected to the CPU to facilitate high-speed communication?
exp:
The Northbridge chipset connects the CPU directly to fast components such as RAM and the graphics bus.
★ Exam Points:
• Northbridge (Memory Controller Hub) links CPU with RAM and AGP/PCIe graphics.
• Southbridge (I/O Controller Hub) handles slower I/O.
• Modern CPUs integrate the Northbridge functions.

q: Consider a computer system with a multi-core processor. What is the primary advantage of having multiple cores compared to a single-core processor with the same clock speed when executing multiple independent tasks simultaneously?
o: Reduced power consumption for the overall system
Increased capacity for the system's main memory (RAM)
Improved ability to handle and execute multiple separate processes concurrently
Enhanced speed for executing a single, heavily threaded application
exp:
Multiple cores can run several separate tasks or threads at the same time, which improves multitasking and parallel execution.
★ Exam Points:
• Multi-core = multiple processing units on one chip.
• Helps parallel and multitasking workloads.
• Single-threaded tasks don't gain much.

q: Which of the following devices can function as both input and output devices?
exp:
A touch screen both displays output and accepts touch input, so it is an input-output device.
★ Exam Points:
• Touch screen is an I/O device.
• Microphone and scanner are input devices.
• Projector is an output device.

q: Which of the following is an example of an input device that allows users to interact with a computer by typing text?
exp:
The keyboard is the input device used to type text.
★ Exam Points:
• Keyboard is the primary text input device.
• QWERTY layout by Christopher Sholes.
• Standard keyboard has 101–104 keys.

q: Which output device is specifically designed to produce high-quality printed graphics and text?
exp:
An inkjet printer produces high-quality printed text and graphics, unlike a dot-matrix printer's coarse impact output.
★ Exam Points:
• Inkjet sprays ink droplets; laser uses toner and a drum.
• Dot-matrix is an impact printer (uses ribbon).
• Printer speed: PPM (pages per minute).

q: Which of the following best encapsulates the fundamental difference between the von Neumann and Harvard architectures in computer systems?
o: Von Neumann uses one shared memory; Harvard can fetch instructions and data simultaneously
Harvard architecture uses a simpler control unit than von Neumann
Von Neumann uses separate address spaces for instructions and data
exp:
In the von Neumann architecture, instructions and data share one memory and bus, so they are fetched one after another (von Neumann bottleneck); the Harvard architecture has separate memories and buses for instructions and data, allowing simultaneous fetching.
★ Exam Points:
• Harvard architecture is used in DSPs and microcontrollers.
• Von Neumann is used in most general-purpose computers.
• Modified Harvard uses split caches with a single main memory.

q: Which of the following components is NOT part of the CPU?
exp:
The CPU consists of the ALU, control unit, registers and cache. A hard disk drive is external secondary storage.
★ Exam Points:
• HDD is secondary storage, outside the CPU.
• Cache (L1/L2/L3) is inside or near the CPU.
• Registers are the fastest memory in the CPU.

q: In modern CPUs, what technique is used to execute multiple instructions simultaneously?
exp:
Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode and execute stages of successive instructions so several instructions are in progress at once.
★ Exam Points:
• Pipelining overlaps fetch, decode and execute stages.
• Superscalar CPUs issue multiple instructions per cycle.
• It increases throughput, not clock speed.

q: What is the primary function of the CPU in a computer system?
exp:
The CPU executes instructions and processes data.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = ALU + CU + registers.
• CPU executes the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
• Clock speed measured in GHz.

q: What is the fundamental difference between a 'cold boot' and a 'warm boot' of a computer system?
o: A cold boot preserves the current state of applications, while a warm boot closes them.
A cold boot restarts the operating system from a powered-off state, while a warm boot restarts it from a running state.
A cold boot is initiated by the user, while a warm boot is initiated by the operating system due to an error.
A cold boot only reloads the kernel, while a warm boot reinitializes all hardware components.
exp:
A cold boot starts the computer from a powered-off state; a warm boot restarts it without cutting power (Ctrl+Alt+Del or Restart).
★ Exam Points:
• Cold (hard) boot – switching on from off state.
• Warm (soft) boot – restart (Ctrl + Alt + Del in DOS era).
• POST runs fully during a cold boot.

q: Which combination correctly matches the device with its primary function?
o: OMR - Detecting shaded marks on paper
exp:
OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) detects shaded marks on paper, such as in exam answer sheets.
★ Exam Points:
• OMR – shaded bubbles (OMR answer sheets).
• MICR – cheque numbers (E-13B font in India).
• Barcode reader – reads bar patterns (UPC/EAN).

q: Which device converts printed text into machine-encoded text using pattern recognition?
exp:
An OCR scanner converts printed text into machine-encoded text using pattern recognition.
★ Exam Points:
• OCR converts scanned text into editable text.
• Used in digitising documents.
• Google Lens uses OCR.

q: The component inside the CPU responsible for arithmetic operations and logical comparisons is the ________.
exp:
The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) inside the CPU performs arithmetic operations and logical comparisons.
★ Exam Points:
• ALU = Arithmetic Logic Unit.
• Logical comparisons: =, <, >.
• ALU works under the control of CU.

q: Which of the following devices can act as both an input as well as an output device?
exp:
Among the options, only the touchscreen acts as both input and output.
★ Exam Points:
• Touchscreen = input + output.
• Plotter is output (large drawings).
• Digital camera and barcode reader are input devices.

q: Which device is designed to integrate processing, memory, and input/output components into one compact unit?
exp:
A microcontroller integrates processor, memory and input/output on one chip.
★ Exam Points:
• Microcontroller = CPU + RAM + ROM + I/O on one chip.
• Used in washing machines, microwaves, cars.
• Examples: Intel 8051, Arduino (ATmega).

q: Which component of the Central Processing Unit (CPU) is responsible for performing calculations and logical comparisons?
exp:
The ALU performs calculations and logical comparisons.
★ Exam Points:
• ALU performs +, −, ×, ÷ and AND, OR, NOT, comparisons.
• Results stored in accumulator/registers.
• CU controls the ALU.

q: The CPU retrieves the upcoming instruction for execution from which system component?
exp:
The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction the CPU will fetch.
★ Exam Points:
• PC is incremented after each fetch.
• Jump/branch instructions change the PC.
• Also called Instruction Pointer (IP) in x86.

q: What does PCB stand for in a Computer System?
exp:
PCB stands for Printed Circuit Board.
★ Exam Points:
• PCB = Printed Circuit Board.
• PCB in OS context = Process Control Block.
• Motherboard is the main PCB.

q: The CPU mainly performs which of the following functions?
exp:
The CPU mainly performs processing and control.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU functions: processing (ALU) and control (CU).
• Storage is done by memory.
• Output by output devices.

q: Which of the following devices performs optical character recognition (OCR)?
exp:
An OCR scanner recognises printed characters and converts them to editable text; barcode readers read bar patterns.
★ Exam Points:
• OCR – Optical Character Recognition.
• OMR – Optical Mark Recognition (bubble sheets).
• MICR – reads magnetic ink on cheques.

q: What does CPU stand for in computer systems?
exp:
CPU = Central Processing Unit.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = Central Processing Unit.
• ALU = Arithmetic Logic Unit.
• CU = Control Unit.

q: Which of the following best describes the role of the Control Unit within the Central Processing Unit?
o: It performs all mathematical and logical calculations.
It displays the processed output to the user.
It stores data and instructions temporarily during processing.
It directs and coordinates the activities of all components of the computer.
exp:
The Control Unit directs and coordinates the operations of the CPU and other components.
★ Exam Points:
• CU directs the operations of the processor.
• It tells memory, ALU and I/O how to respond.
• Output is shown by output devices.

q: Which of the following accurately represents the two main components of the CPU and their functions?
o: Monitor and Keyboard – Control the speed of data processing
RAM and ROM – Store data and instructions permanently
HDD and SSD – Perform data input and output tasks
ALU and CU – Perform calculations and control all computer operations
exp:
The two main components of the CPU are the ALU (arithmetic and logic) and the CU (control).
★ Exam Points:
• ALU – calculations and comparisons.
• CU – control and coordination.
• Registers – temporary high-speed storage.

q: Which of the following pairs correctly classifies one input and one output device?
o: Joystick – Output device, Speaker – Input device
Microphone – Input device, Monitor – Output device
Keyboard – Output device, Printer – Input device
Mouse – Output device, Scanner – Input device
exp:
A microphone is an input device and a monitor is an output device.
★ Exam Points:
• Input: keyboard, mouse, microphone, scanner, joystick.
• Output: monitor, printer, speaker, projector.
• I/O: touchscreen, modem.

q: Which of the following are main subsystems of the Central Processing Unit (CPU)?
o: Control Unit, Arithmetic Unit and Logic Unit
Arithmetic Unit, Memory Unit and Output Unit
Logic Unit, Input Unit and Storage Unit
Arithmetic Unit, Graphics Unit and Control Bus
exp:
The CPU's main subsystems are the Control Unit and the Arithmetic Logic Unit (arithmetic unit and logic unit).
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = CU + ALU (+ registers).
• ALU = arithmetic unit + logic unit.
• Memory unit is separate (primary memory).

q: Which of the following is the function of the Central Processing Unit (CPU) in a computer?
o: It sends output to printers and monitors.
It receives input from the keyboard and mouse only.
It processes data and controls operations of all parts of the computer.
It stores all user files permanently.
exp:
The CPU processes data and controls the operations of all parts of the computer.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU processes data and controls all parts.
• Input comes through input devices.
• Permanent storage is on HDD/SSD.

q: What is the primary function of the Control Unit within a CPU?
o: Directing the flow of instructions and data
exp:
The Control Unit directs the flow of instructions and data in the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• CU fetches, decodes and controls execution.
• It sends control signals to memory, ALU and I/O.
• CU itself does not process data.

q: Which computer port provides high-speed serial transfer, power supply and plug-and-play support for keyboards, printers and storage?
exp:
USB (Universal Serial Bus) is hot-pluggable, supplies power and supports many devices.
★ Exam Points:
• USB 1.0 launched in 1996.
• USB-C is reversible.
• USB4 reaches up to 40–80 Gbps.

q:
Which statements about the CPU are correct?
1. The CPU is often referred to as the ‘brain’ of the computer.
2. The CPU consists of three main units: Control Unit, ALU and cache memory.
exp:
The CPU is called the brain (1 is true); its main units are the CU, ALU and registers/memory unit – cache is not counted as one of the three main units.
★ Exam Points:
• Registers are inside the CPU.
• Cache may be on the CPU chip but is a memory, not a processing unit.
• CU directs operations; ALU calculates.

q:
Select whether the statements about the CPU are true or false.
(i) The CPU's clock speed controls the timing and execution speed of instructions.
(ii) The CPU's cache memory provides high-speed access to frequently used instructions and data.
exp:
Both statements are correct.
★ Exam Points:
• Clock speed is measured in GHz.
• Cache levels: L1, L2, L3.
• More cores + higher clock = more performance.

q: The ____ holds the address of the active memory location.
exp:
The MAR holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to.
★ Exam Points:
• MDR/MBR holds the data being transferred.
• PC holds the address of the next instruction.
• Stack Pointer holds the address of the top of the stack.

q: ____ are a set of wires that carry a group of bits in parallel with an associated control scheme, providing a communication path between two or more devices of a computer.
exp:
A bus is a group of parallel wires used to transfer data, addresses and control signals between components.
★ Exam Points:
• System bus = Data bus + Address bus + Control bus.
• Address bus is unidirectional; data bus is bidirectional.
• Bus width decides how many bits move at once.

q: Which among the following ports is also called the mouse port?
exp:
The PS/2 port (6-pin mini-DIN) was used for mouse (green) and keyboard (purple).
★ Exam Points:
• PS/2 introduced by IBM in 1987.
• FireWire = IEEE 1394 (Apple).
• Today USB is used for mouse and keyboard.

q: Which among the following statements is incorrect about the Central Processing Unit?
o: Control Unit controls the order in which instructions enter and leave the processor and how they are executed.
Arithmetic Logic Unit is also known as the mathematical brain of a computer.
Control Unit directs and manages operation sequences.
Arithmetic Logic Unit is responsible for taking input, converting it into a signal and storing it for further processing.
exp:
The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations; taking input and converting it into signals is the job of input devices/units, not the ALU.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU = ALU + CU + Registers.
• CU is called the "nerve centre" of the computer.
• CPU is called the brain of the computer.

q: ____ is a reading device that reads printed text by scanning it character by character.
exp:
OCR recognises printed or handwritten characters from a scanned image and converts them into editable text.
★ Exam Points:
• MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques.
• OMR reads marks on answer sheets.
• Digitizer converts drawings into digital form.

q: A ____ port transmits one bit of a byte at a time as a single stream of bits and is meant for transmitting slow data over long distances.
exp:
A serial port (COM/RS-232) sends data one bit at a time over a single line, which is suitable for long distances.
★ Exam Points:
• Parallel ports send 8 bits simultaneously over short distances.
• Serial port commonly uses a 9-pin (DB-9) connector.
• USB is also serial but much faster.

q: Which register in the instruction cycle holds the last instruction fetched?
exp:
The Instruction Register holds the instruction just fetched from memory while it is being decoded and executed.
★ Exam Points:
• PC holds the address of the next instruction.
• Instruction cycle: Fetch → Decode → Execute (→ Store).
• MBR/MDR holds data read from or written to memory.

q: ____ is the oldest type of Central Processing Unit (CPU).
exp:
Early processors had only one core that executed one instruction stream at a time; multi-core CPUs came later (dual-core from 2005).
★ Exam Points:
• A core is an independent processing unit within a CPU.
• Intel 4004 (1971) was the first microprocessor.
• Multi-core CPUs improve multitasking and parallel processing.

q: Which among the following ports is also known as the Line Printer Port?
exp:
The parallel port (LPT – Line Print Terminal) was used mainly to connect printers; it sends 8 bits at a time.
★ Exam Points:
• Parallel port uses a 25-pin DB-25 connector.
• Serial port (COM) sends one bit at a time.
• USB has replaced both serial and parallel ports.

q: Which among the following devices is also known as a Visual Display Unit (VDU)?
exp:
The monitor is called the VDU because it visually displays output (soft copy).
★ Exam Points:
• Monitor types: CRT, LCD, LED, OLED, Plasma.
• Printer gives hard copy output.
• Screen size is measured diagonally in inches.

q: The instruction that is not to be executed immediately is placed in the ____.
exp:
In the IAS (von Neumann) machine two instructions are fetched together; the one not needed immediately waits in the Instruction Buffer Register.
★ Exam Points:
• PC holds the address of the next instruction.
• MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed; MBR/MDR holds the data.
• CIR/IR holds the instruction currently being executed.

q: ____ is a high-speed device used in the CPU that is utilised to store data temporarily during processing.
exp:
Registers are small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold data, instructions and addresses being processed.
★ Exam Points:
• Registers are the fastest memory in a computer.
• Order of speed: Registers > Cache > RAM > Secondary storage.
• Examples: PC, IR, MAR, MDR, Accumulator.

q: Video Graphics Array (VGA) connectors, which connect the monitor to a computer's video card, have ____ holes.
exp:
A standard VGA (DE-15) connector has 15 pins/holes arranged in three rows of five.
★ Exam Points:
• VGA was introduced by IBM in 1987; it carries an analog signal.
• DVI and HDMI are digital video interfaces.
• HDMI carries both audio and video.

q: What is the role of "hardware handshaking" (such as using RTS/CTS lines) in asynchronous serial communication?
o: Providing error detection using parity bits
Preventing data loss by managing buffer overflow
Synchronizing internal clocks of both devices
exp:
In asynchronous serial communication (such as RS-232 / UART), hardware handshaking uses dedicated control lines —RTS (Request to Send) and CTS (Clear to Send)—for flow control so a fast transmitter pauses when the receiver's buffer is nearly full, preventing buffer overflow and data loss.
★ Exam Points:
• Software flow control (XON/XOFF) uses special ASCII control characters (DC1 = 0x11, DC3 = 0x13) inside the data stream instead of extra wires.
• Asynchronous transmission frames each byte with a Start bit (0) and Stop bit(s) (1) without a shared clock line.
• Parity bit (Even/Odd) is used for 1-bit error detection, not flow control.

q: When comparing HDMI and DisplayPort, which feature is found exclusively in DisplayPort architecture?
exp:
Daisy Chaining via Multi-Stream Transport (MST)—introduced in DisplayPort 1.2—is exclusive to DisplayPort architecture, allowing multiple independent monitors to be connected in series from a single DisplayPort output on the computer.
★ Exam Points:
• Feature | DisplayPort | HDMI
• Daisy Chaining (MST) | Supported (DP 1.2+) | Not natively supported
• TMDS Signaling | Packetized micro-packets (LVDS/lanes) | Used in HDMI (up to 2.0; FRL in 2.1)
• Primary Target | PC monitors, high refresh & multi-display | TVs, home theatre, consoles & PCs
• Both HDMI and DisplayPort carry uncompressed digital video and multi-channel audio over a single cable.

q: During the instruction cycle, which specific register holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed by the CPU?
exp:
During the fetch-decode-execute cycle, the Instruction Register (IR) holds the binary machine instruction that has just been fetched from memory and is currently being decoded and executed by the CPU's Control Unit.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU Register | Exact Function
• Program Counter (PC) | Holds the memory address of the NEXT instruction to fetch
• Memory Address Register (MAR) | Holds the memory address currently being read from or written to
• Memory Buffer / Data Register (MBR/MDR) | Holds data or instruction fetched from or sent to memory
• Instruction Register (IR) | Holds the CURRENT instruction being decoded and executed
• Accumulator (AC) | Stores intermediate arithmetic and logic results from the ALU

q: What is the primary architectural advantage of a microprogrammed control unit compared to a hardwired control unit?
exp:
In a microprogrammed control unit, control signals are generated from microinstructions stored in special control memory (CM) rather than fixed logic circuitry. Hence, its biggest architectural advantage over a hardwired unit is the ease and flexibility of modifying or updating instruction sets simply by updating microcode.
★ Exam Points:
• Hardwired Control Unit uses fixed combinational logic gates/flip-flops—it is faster (used in RISC processors) but difficult and costly to modify.
• Microprogrammed Control Unit (introduced by Maurice Wilkes in 1951) is slower due to control-memory access but ideal for complex instruction sets (CISC).

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of touchscreen?
exp:
Gas plasma is a display technology; touchscreen types are resistive, capacitive, surface acoustic wave and infrared.
★ Exam Points:
• Smartphones use capacitive touchscreens.
• Resistive screens respond to pressure (stylus works).
• A touchscreen is both an input and output device.

q: Which type of computer memory loses its stored data when the power supply is turned off?
exp:
Volatile memory (like RAM) loses its contents when the power supply is switched off.
★ Exam Points:
• RAM and cache are volatile.
• ROM, flash, HDD are non-volatile.
• Save work regularly to avoid loss.

q: Which characteristic best differentiates Static RAM (SRAM) from Dynamic RAM (DRAM), leading to SRAM being used for CPU cache and DRAM for main system memory (RAM)?
o: DRAM is located directly on the CPU die, while SRAM is located on the motherboard.
DRAM is non-volatile, while SRAM is volatile.
SRAM is significantly faster, more expensive, and consumes less power than DRAM.
SRAM requires constant refreshing to hold data, while DRAM does not.
exp:
SRAM is much faster, more expensive and less dense than DRAM and needs no refreshing, so it is used for CPU cache while cheaper DRAM is used for main memory.
★ Exam Points:
• SRAM uses flip-flops (6 transistors per bit).
• DRAM uses one capacitor + one transistor per bit.
• DRAM must be refreshed periodically.

q: Data stored on a hard disk must be transferred to which memory unit before the CPU can access it?
exp:
Data from the hard disk must be loaded into primary memory (RAM) before the CPU can use it.
★ Exam Points:
• CPU accesses only primary memory directly.
• Data moves HDD → RAM → cache → registers.
• Secondary memory is slower.

q: Which type of memory is non-volatile and is used to store essential system instructions in a computer?
exp:
ROM is non-volatile and stores essential system instructions.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM is non-volatile memory.
• Registers, RAM and cache are volatile.
• ROM contents are written by the manufacturer.

q: In the context of computer hardware components, what is the primary function of ROM?
o: It physically supports all internal hardware modules.
It holds essential firmware required for booting the system.
It stores temporary data used during system processing.
It executes programs and handles arithmetic operations.
exp:
ROM holds the essential firmware needed for booting the system.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM holds BIOS/UEFI firmware.
• ROM is non-volatile.
• Types: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM.

q: Where are files and folders typically stored in a computer?
exp:
Files and folders are stored on the hard drive.
★ Exam Points:
• Hard drive is the main permanent storage.
• SSDs are replacing HDDs.
• Files are organised in folders by the file system.

q: Which of the following scenarios would most likely result in a 'page fault' error during typical computer operation?
o: Accessing data stored in the CPU cache
Writing data to a read-only memory location
Attempting to access a memory address that has been swapped out to the hard drive
Executing an instruction directly from the BIOS
exp:
A page fault occurs when a program tries to access a memory page that is not currently in RAM (e.g., it was swapped out to disk), so the OS must load it from virtual memory.
★ Exam Points:
• Page faults are handled by the OS.
• Frequent page faults cause thrashing.
• Pages are fixed-size blocks of memory.

q: Which of the following memory types is also called solid-state storage?
exp:
Flash memory (SSD, USB, memory cards) is solid-state storage with no moving parts.
★ Exam Points:
• Flash memory is non-volatile EEPROM type.
• Used in SSDs, pen drives, memory cards.
• Invented by Fujio Masuoka (Toshiba).

q: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about Cache Memory?
o: Cache memory is a form of secondary storage.
Cache memory stores frequently accessed data for quick retrieval.
Cache memory is faster than main memory.
Cache memory is located close to or inside the CPU.
exp:
Cache memory is not secondary storage; it is a very fast memory close to the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• Cache is primary-level memory, not secondary.
• Cache sits between CPU and RAM.
• Secondary storage: HDD, SSD.

q: What is the full form of CD, commonly used in storage devices?
exp:
CD stands for Compact Disc.
★ Exam Points:
• CD = Compact Disc (developed by Philips and Sony, 1982).
• CD capacity ≈ 700 MB / 80 minutes audio.
• CD-R is write-once; CD-RW is rewritable.

q: Which of the following statements best describes the role of RAM and ROM in a computer system?
o: RAM is used to store the operating system and permanent files, while ROM is used to store temporary data.
ROM is used to store system firmware, while RAM stores temporary data for active processes.
ROM is used for storing data that can be modified and written to, while RAM stores fixed data.
RAM is non-volatile, while ROM is volatile.
exp:
ROM stores firmware (boot instructions), while RAM temporarily stores running programs and data.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM stores firmware like BIOS.
• RAM stores currently running programs.
• Both are primary memory.

q: Which of the following statements about RAM and ROM with reference to computer memory is correct?
o: RAM is non-volatile, while ROM is volatile.
RAM cannot be written to, only read from.
RAM temporarily stores data for active programs, while ROM permanently stores firmware.
exp:
RAM is volatile and holds data for running programs; ROM is non-volatile and holds permanent instructions.
★ Exam Points:
• RAM – volatile, read/write.
• ROM – non-volatile, mostly read-only.
• RAM is faster to write than ROM.

q: What are the wavelength and type of the laser used in a standard CD-ROM drive?
exp:
A standard CD-ROM drive uses an infrared laser of about 780 nm; DVDs use a 650 nm red laser and Blu-ray a 405 nm blue-violet laser.
★ Exam Points:
• CD: 780 nm infrared laser (~700 MB).
• DVD: 650 nm red laser (4.7 GB).
• Blu-ray: 405 nm blue-violet laser (25 GB per layer).

q: In a multitasking operating system, what role does RAM primarily play when multiple applications are open simultaneously?
o: It acts as permanent storage for installed software.
It temporarily holds active program data and instructions to enable fast switching between tasks.
It queues printing tasks before they reach the printer.
It processes user input commands from external devices like keyboard or mouse.
exp:
In a multitasking OS, RAM temporarily holds the data and instructions of all active programs so the CPU can switch between them quickly.
★ Exam Points:
• More RAM allows more open applications.
• When RAM is full, virtual memory is used.
• RAM is volatile.

q: What is the primary purpose of virtual memory in a computer system?
o: To extend CACHE memory for storage
To extend RAM capacity by using disk space
exp:
Virtual memory extends the usable RAM by using part of the disk as additional memory space.
★ Exam Points:
• Virtual memory uses disk (page file/swap) as extra RAM.
• Page fault occurs when needed page is not in RAM.
• Thrashing = excessive paging.

q: What is the main purpose of cache memory in a computer?
o: To store frequently accessed data for quick retrieval
exp:
Cache memory stores frequently accessed data and instructions for quick retrieval by the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• Cache is SRAM-based and very fast.
• Levels: L1, L2, L3.
• Cache hit improves performance.

q: What type of memory is used to store data temporarily while a computer is running?
exp:
RAM temporarily stores data and programs while the computer is running.
★ Exam Points:
• RAM is volatile primary memory.
• RAM types: SRAM and DRAM.
• Data is lost when power goes off.

q: The term ROM is an abbreviation for:
exp:
ROM stands for Read Only Memory.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM = Read Only Memory.
• Types: Mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM.
• BIOS is stored in ROM.

q: RAM and ROM belong to which broader category?
exp:
RAM and ROM are primary (main) memory.
★ Exam Points:
• Primary memory: RAM, ROM (and cache).
• Secondary memory: HDD, SSD, CD.
• Primary memory is directly accessed by CPU.

q: In a computer system, a running program stores currently required data in RAM. What does RAM stand for?
exp:
RAM stands for Random Access Memory.
★ Exam Points:
• RAM = Random Access Memory.
• Any location can be accessed directly.
• DDR4/DDR5 are common RAM types.

q: Which memory is fastest and located inside the CPU?
exp:
Registers are the fastest memory and are inside the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• Memory speed: Registers > Cache > RAM > SSD > HDD.
• Registers are inside the CPU.
• Cache L1 is the fastest cache.

q: Which feature distinguishes ROM from RAM?
o: ROM stores permanent instructions; RAM stores temporary data.
ROM is used for storage; RAM is used for graphics.
ROM is volatile; RAM is non-volatile.
exp:
ROM stores permanent instructions, while RAM stores temporary data.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM – permanent; RAM – temporary.
• RAM is faster for read/write.
• Graphics memory is VRAM.

q: Which of the following memory types is non- volatile?
exp:
ROM is non-volatile; RAM is volatile, and CPU and PCB are not memory types.
★ Exam Points:
• Non-volatile: ROM, flash, HDD, SSD.
• Volatile: RAM, cache, registers.
• PCB is a circuit board, not memory.

q: Which of the following is true for Read-Only Memory (ROM)?
o: It is volatile memory that stores data temporarily.
It stores data that can be modified by the user.
It stores the booting instructions permanently.
exp:
ROM stores the booting instructions and is non-volatile.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM stores BIOS/boot instructions permanently.
• ROM is non-volatile.
• Processing is done by the CPU.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with both its abbreviation and its function?
o: ROM – Read Only Memory – Stores boot instructions needed when the computer is powered on
PCB – Printed Chip Base – Transfers data from CPU to display
CPU – Central Processing Unit – Stores user files permanently
RAM – Read Access Memory – Runs the operating system even after power is
exp:
ROM (Read Only Memory) stores the boot instructions needed to start the computer; the other pairs have wrong expansions or functions.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM = Read Only Memory (stores BIOS/boot program).
• RAM = Random Access Memory (not Read Access).
• PCB = Printed Circuit Board.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of primary memory in a computer?
o: It holds data temporarily for quick access during processing.
It is slower than secondary memory.
It is used to back up files externally.
exp:
Primary memory holds data and instructions temporarily for quick access by the CPU during processing.
★ Exam Points:
• Primary memory is faster but smaller than secondary.
• RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile.
• Backup is done on secondary storage.

q: What does the abbreviation 'SRAM' stand for in computer memory?
exp:
SRAM stands for Static Random Access Memory.
★ Exam Points:
• SRAM = Static RAM, used for cache.
• DRAM = Dynamic RAM, used for main memory.
• SRAM does not need refreshing.

q: Which type of memory loses all its stored data when the power is turned off?
exp:
RAM is volatile and loses its data when power is turned off.
★ Exam Points:
• RAM loses data on power off (volatile).
• ROM, HDD, USB drives keep data.
• UPS prevents data loss during power cuts.

q: A memory chip stores 8 MB of data. How many bytes does it contain (binary measurement)?
exp:
1 MB = 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes; 8 × 1,048,576 = 8,388,608 bytes.
★ Exam Points:
• 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
• 1 GB = 1024 MB.
• Decimal MB (10^6) is used by disk makers.

q: ROM is primarily used for which purpose?
exp:
ROM stores firmware like BIOS/UEFI that starts the computer.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM is non-volatile and mostly read-only.
• Types: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM.
• RAM provides temporary storage.

q: Which type of ROM can be electronically erased and reprogrammed?
exp:
EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM) can be erased and rewritten using electrical signals.
★ Exam Points:
• EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light.
• PROM can be programmed only once.
• Flash memory is a type of EEPROM.

q: What is the primary reason DRAM needs to be refreshed periodically?
o: To allow the CPU to access new data
To prevent data corruption caused by magnetic fields
To recharge the capacitors storing data bits
exp:
Each DRAM bit is stored as charge in a tiny capacitor that leaks, so it must be refreshed thousands of times per second.
★ Exam Points:
• SRAM uses flip-flops and needs no refresh.
• DRAM is cheaper and denser than SRAM.
• DDR4/DDR5 are types of SDRAM.

q:
Which statements about computer memory are correct?
1. RAM is volatile memory, meaning it loses data when power is turned off.
2. ROM stores essential instructions required for the computer to boot.
exp:
Both are correct: RAM is volatile and ROM holds firmware (BIOS/UEFI) needed for booting.
★ Exam Points:
• ROM is non-volatile.
• BIOS performs POST at start-up.
• RAM is the main working memory.

q: Which among the following is NOT a magnetic storage?
exp:
A memory card (SD, microSD) uses flash memory – a semiconductor storage, not magnetic.
★ Exam Points:
• Magnetic storage: HDD, floppy disk, magnetic tape.
• Optical storage: CD, DVD, Blu-ray.
• Flash storage: SSD, pen drive, memory card.

q: Which of the following is also known as a flash drive?
exp:
A pen drive (USB flash drive / thumb drive) uses flash memory and connects through a USB port.
★ Exam Points:
• Flash memory is a type of EEPROM.
• Pen drives are non-volatile and portable.
• First USB flash drives appeared around 2000.

q: ____ memory supplies data and instructions to the CPU at a rapid rate.
exp:
Cache memory is a small, very fast memory (SRAM) between CPU and RAM that holds frequently used data so the CPU can get it quickly.
★ Exam Points:
• Cache levels: L1 (fastest, smallest), L2, L3.
• Cache uses SRAM; main memory uses DRAM.
• Cache hit = data found in cache; cache miss = not found.

q: ____ is a dedicated file storage device that provides LAN users with centralised, consolidated disk storage through a standard Ethernet connection.
exp:
NAS is a storage device connected to the network that lets multiple users share files over Ethernet.
★ Exam Points:
• SAN (Storage Area Network) gives block-level storage over a dedicated network.
• NAS provides file-level storage.
• DAS = Direct Attached Storage (connected to one computer).

q: Which among the following statements is incorrect about secondary memory?
o: A computer may run without secondary memory.
It is known as backup memory.
Data is permanently stored even if power is switched off.
exp:
Secondary memory (HDD, SSD, CD) is non-volatile; volatile memory such as RAM loses data when power is off.
★ Exam Points:
• Secondary memory is slower but cheaper and larger than primary memory.
• It is not directly accessed by the CPU.
• Examples: hard disk, pen drive, optical discs, magnetic tape.

q: Which among the following is incorrect about cache memory?
o: It is slower than the main memory.
It acts as a high-speed buffer between CPU and main memory.
It stores data in temporary use.
It keeps the programs that can be run in a short amount of time.
exp:
Cache memory is faster (and costlier) than main memory; that is why it is used as a buffer for the CPU.
★ Exam Points:
• Cache is volatile and made of SRAM.
• Cache size is small (KB to MB).
• Locality of reference makes cache effective.

q: Which of the following is NOT a magnetic disk?
exp:
A DVD is an optical disc read by laser; Winchester disk (hard disk), Zip disk and disk pack are magnetic.
★ Exam Points:
• Winchester disk is the old name of the hard disk (IBM).
• DVD capacity: 4.7 GB (single layer).
• Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser (405 nm).

q: ____ is also known as an electronic disk.
exp:
A Solid-State Drive stores data on flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it is called an electronic (silicon) disk.
★ Exam Points:
• SSDs are faster, quieter and more shock-resistant than HDDs.
• SSDs use NAND flash memory (non-volatile).
• Interfaces: SATA and NVMe (PCIe).

q: The memory unit that communicates directly with the CPU is called ____ memory.
exp:
Main (primary) memory – RAM and ROM – is directly accessed by the CPU; auxiliary memory must first be loaded into main memory.
★ Exam Points:
• Primary memory is also called internal memory.
• Secondary/auxiliary memory: HDD, SSD, CD, pen drive.
• Cache acts as a high-speed buffer between CPU and main memory.

q: In enterprise storage, how does a "Copy-on-Write (CoW) snapshot" differ from traditional backups?
o: It stores only pointers to data blocks until modifications are made to those blocks.
It is stored on a physically separate secondary storage device.
It immediately creates a full bit-by-bit copy (clone) of the data.
The system must go offline during this process.
exp:
In enterprise storage, a Copy-on-Write (CoW) snapshot is created almost instantaneously because it initially stores only metadata pointers to the existing data blocks. Only when a block is about to be modified is its original content copied to the snapshot reserve area.
★ Exam Points:
• Because CoW snapshots depend on the source volume's unchanged blocks, they are not a substitute for an independent off-site backup if the physical disk array fails.
• Redirect-on-Write (RoW) writes new modified data directly to a new block location and keeps the original block untouched for the snapshot.
• Traditional full backups create a complete physical duplicate on separate media and take much longer.

q: A computer system has a memory capacity of 4K × 8 bits. How many address lines are required on the address bus to uniquely identify each byte in this memory?
exp:
The memory organization is 4K×8 bits, which means there are 4K addressable words and each word is 8 bits = 1 byte: Number of memory locations (N) = 4×1024 = 4096 = 2² × 2¹⁰ = 2¹² To uniquely address 2¹² byte locations, the address bus requires 12 address lines.
★ Exam Points:
• General formula: If memory has 2ⁿ addressable units, then Address lines = n (i.e., log N). 2
• Since word size is 8 bits, the Data Bus width is 8 lines.
• Quick powers of 2: 1K = 2¹⁰ (10 lines), 4K = 2¹² (12 lines), 64K = 2¹⁶ (16 lines), 1M = 2²⁰ (20 lines), 1G = 2³⁰ (30 lines).

q: What is the primary purpose of using file compression techniques before uploading to cloud storage?
o: Making the file readable on various devices
Converting the file into a secure format
Reducing file size and saving storage space
exp:
Applying file compression (such as ZIP, RAR, or 7z) removes redundant bit patterns so files occupy fewer bytes, reducing file size, saving cloud storage space, and speeding up upload/download transfers.
★ Exam Points:
• Lossless compression (ZIP, PNG, FLAC) reconstructs the exact original file bit-for-bit—essential for documents, spreadsheets, and code.
• Lossy compression (JPEG, MP3, MP4) discards impercep-tible details to achieve much smaller file sizes for media.
• Compression alone does not encrypt data unless password-based encryption (e.g., AES-256 in 7z/ZIP) is explicitly enabled.

q: A user works on a Word document from a removable drive and forgets to copy it back to a main storage location. The drive is later misplaced. Which concept has been ignored?
o: The importance of maintaining backup copies in stable locations
Cloud synchronisation keeps a copy on the remote service that can be downloaded again
exp:
Failing to duplicate data onto primary stable storage creates absolute reliance on vulnerable hardware. This scenario highlights a neglect of backup redundancy protocols, which prevent permanent data loss caused by lost or dam-aged physical media.
★ Exam Points:
• Removable storage drives (USB flash drives) have higher physical loss and failure rates.
• Cloud auto-syncing automatically mirrors local updates to secure remote cloud servers.
• Critical document management requires keeping primary and redundant backup copies.
• Data loss risks can be mitigated using scheduled automated backup tools.

q:
Identify whether the given statements about computer memory are true or false.
(i) Auxiliary memory holds programs and data for future use because it is non-volatile.
(ii) The most common forms of auxiliary storage devices are cache and RAM chips.
exp:
Auxiliary memory is non-volatile and stores data for future use; cache and RAM are primary (volatile) memory, not auxiliary storage.
★ Exam Points:
• Common auxiliary storage: HDD, SSD, optical disc, pen drive.
• Auxiliary memory is also called secondary memory.
• It is not directly accessed by the CPU.

q: Which of the following is an optical storage device?
exp:
A CD is read and written using a laser beam, so it is optical storage.
★ Exam Points:
• CD capacity: about 700 MB; uses 780 nm infrared laser.
• Floppy, tape and HDD are magnetic storage.
• CD was developed by Philips and Sony.

q: Which of these examples best represents a category of utility software?
exp:
Disk Cleanup is utility software that maintains and optimises the system.
★ Exam Points:
• Utilities: Disk Cleanup, Defragmenter, antivirus, backup.
• Utilities maintain and optimise the computer.
• PowerPoint, Excel, Word are applications.

q: Which of the following is an example of application software that depends entirely on system software to function?
exp:
Microsoft Word is application software that depends on system software to run.
★ Exam Points:
• Applications need an OS to run.
• Linux kernel, BIOS and Ubuntu are system software.
• Word is part of MS Office.

q: Which classification best describes a compiler based on its role in program translation?
o: Application software because it edits documents
Application software because users launch it manually
It is a hardware abstraction layer
System software because it converts code for OS execution
exp:
A compiler translates high-level code into machine code; it is system software (a language processor).
★ Exam Points:
• Compilers, interpreters and assemblers are language translators (system software).
• Compiler translates the whole program at once.
• Output of a compiler is object code.

q: Which of the following is an example of Application Software?
exp:
MS Excel is application software; BIOS, Linux and Windows are system software.
★ Exam Points:
• Application software: MS Office, browsers, games.
• System software: Windows, Linux, BIOS.
• Excel is a spreadsheet application.

q: Which of the following best describes an operating system?
o: A program used to watch videos
A program used to access the internet
A program that manages memory, processes, and devices
A program used for data entry
exp:
An operating system manages memory, processes and devices.
★ Exam Points:
• OS manages memory, processes, devices and files.
• OS provides the user interface.
• First OS concepts: GM-NAA I/O (1956).

q: Items such as the operating system and device drivers fall under which category of software?
exp:
The operating system and device drivers are system software.
★ Exam Points:
• System software: OS, device drivers, utilities, firmware, language translators.
• Application software performs user tasks.
• Drivers connect OS with hardware.

q: Which of the following is an example of Customized Software?
exp:
School Management Software is built for a specific institution, so it is customised software.
★ Exam Points:
• Customised (tailor-made) software is built for a specific user/organisation.
• Packaged/general-purpose software is for everyone.
• Examples of packaged: MS Office, Photoshop.

q: Which of the following operating systems provides the highest level of user control over system resources and is most commonly used for professional software development on desktops and laptops?
exp:
Linux (Ubuntu, Fedora) gives developers the greatest control over system resources and is open source.
★ Exam Points:
• Linux is open source and highly customisable.
• Popular distros: Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian.
• India's BOSS Linux by C-DAC.

q: Which of the following is an example of an open-source desktop Operating System?
exp:
Ubuntu is an open-source Linux desktop OS; Windows and macOS are proprietary, and Android is mobile-focused.
★ Exam Points:
• Open-source OS: Linux, FreeBSD.
• Proprietary: Windows, macOS.
• Android is based on Linux but mobile-focused.

q: Which of the following Operating System concepts is most directly involved in ensuring that multiple processes can access and modify files concurrently without causing data corruption?
exp:
File locking prevents several processes from modifying the same file at once, avoiding data corruption.
★ Exam Points:
• File locking prevents simultaneous conflicting writes.
• Paging divides memory into pages.
• Scheduling allots CPU time.

q: Considering the fundamental operations of a computer, what is the immediate effect of pressing the Tab key within a command-line interface (CLI) or terminal?
o: It executes the currently typed command.
It switches to a different virtual terminal or console.
It attempts to auto-complete the currently typed command or filename.
It deletes the last typed character.
exp:
In a command-line terminal, Tab auto-completes the command or file name being typed.
★ Exam Points:
• Tab completion saves typing in terminals.
• Pressing Tab twice lists possibilities.
• Enter executes the command.

q: What is the significance of the 'root directory' in a hierarchical file system structure?
o: It is a temporary directory used by the operating system for caching frequently accessed files.
It is a special directory that contains essential operating system kernel files.
It is the directory where all user-specific files are stored.
It is the topmost directory in the file system hierarchy, from which all other directories branch.
exp:
The root directory is the top-level directory of the file system, from which all others branch.
★ Exam Points:
